title: Learning to film game trailers is helping me find bugs/issues I could've missed
author: fapfap_ahh
selftext:
https://reddit.com/link/1xgfdqr/video/ut3r7jlmwwxh1/player

I've been building skills and tools to direct Claude to be able to record/edit/compile trailers for my game. It's a repetitive and iterative process, it helps expand my own creativity so that I can feed it back into the game based on the video spat out. 



Basically, I start with a spreadsheet of scenes that I've come up with that have gameplay and features, plus, few music tracks. 



Claude sequences the music files and produces rises, falls, bpm, and whatnot to see which one fits the scenes best (and what order the scenes go best in). It then checks each visual scene (and it's part) with headless GPU renders, then screenshots, then does recording if the previous steps were good. Final review is from me per scene. 



Best thing? Claude checking headless renders or me watching it record the same moments few times showed me bugs a player would actually hit. 



\- Leave the radar console with a contact investigation page open, and the screen was blank when you came back

\- Animals and side quest humanoids walked straight through tree branches

\- The owl flew through tree tops

\- Wind sound played in still air not just when it was actually windy.

\- Footsteps played during some cutscenes like feeding the heater



The other great thing was showing me how I was still missing some immersion in the game. In one of the scenes, I kept seeing a deer, a boar and a bear within 20m of each other, all ignoring each other. Not very real lol.



So I came up with a design on a "wildlife food chain system" and this is the first pass at directing Claude on implementing it:



\- Deer bolt from wolves and bears

\- A wolf or bear hunts at most once a day, and only where the player can see it.

\- The wolf howls as it sets off. It creeps in, then runs its prey down, or gives up when the prey is quicker.

\- A catch is a kill or a wound. A wounded animal runs on, bleeding leaving a trail for you (or the predator) to follow.

\- After a kill it feeds and guards it. Get too close and it charges you to protect its kill.

\- No free meat for the user if a predator fed on it.

\- Next up, putting wolves and deer in roaming (and communicative) herds



You can see this posted trailer showed some new bugs: owl still hitting flying through the first tree due to it's first flight animation. Those are enxt to quash!

I'm still iterating through and polishing for immersion, plus fixing more edge case bugs, but this has been a great learning strategy for me though and wanted to share it with ya'll!

comments.author: TraplineStudio
comments.body: Does the scene spreadsheet double as a test list now? If Claude replays every scene after each build, a scene that breaks is basically a failing test, and you get fresh trailer footage when they all pass.

replies.author: fapfap_ahh
replies.body:
Yes in a few ways! Scenes (or parts of scenes) can become tests, but, they try to use existing tests to build on first. If the existing ones fails for the scenario, opportunity to improve it or add more!

All of these are selectively tagged and included in build lanes depending on the type of change before a playable build is compiled. Fast lane for tiny changes, quick lane for minor medium, full lane for big changes. 

There's also hooks that can be flipped on for GPU renders or screenshots for Claude to analyze as the lanes are ran (as needed)
